justification: The only human genetic association evidence is the EPIGEN multicentre candidate-gene case-control study (PMID 17913586), which flagged KCNMB4 variation only through set-association analysis in an apparently population-specific manner and explicitly called the findings tentative; a well-powered replication attempt in mTLE failed to confirm rs398702 (PMID 23623847). No articles report pathogenic KCNMB4 variants segregating in probands or families, and the 12q15 microdeletion reports (PMIDs 28159701, 30768759) span multiple genes and actually point to CNOT2, so they cannot establish causality. Strong supporting biology exists but is non-human/in vitro: seizure-induced downregulation of KCNMB4 and increased seizure sensitivity in heterozygous β4 knockout mice (PMID 29145442), and β-subunit-specific modulation of a BK channel epilepsy/dyskinesia mutation (PMID 19204046), with β4 shaping channel pharmacology and trafficking (PMIDs 10792058, 24486049). Hence probability is split nearly evenly between "Existing" (one credible but unreplicated human association) and "Hypothesized" (compelling mechanistic/animal data), with Established effectively excluded.

justification: Human linkage analysis in childhood absence epilepsy families gave positive heterogeneity LOD scores at CACNG3 on 16p12-p13.1 (PMID 11904235), and a follow-up study in 65 nuclear families plus 217 trios found a significant HLOD of 3.54 and transmission disequilibrium for SNPs in a 35 kb region spanning the 5'UTR/exon 1 (PMID 17264864), supporting CACNG3 as a susceptibility locus. However, re-sequencing identified no coding or clearly causal variants, so the evidence is associative rather than causal, and no second independent study reports pathogenic variants in probands or families. Reviews (PMID 22206818) simply restate this association as background and do not add independent evidence; the iPSC transcriptomic study (PMID 34525970) and brain-volume GWAS (PMID 40568677) are not epilepsy-variant evidence, and the PKC study (PMID 17952630) explicitly excluded CACNG3 for a different phenotype. This places the relationship squarely in the "Existing" category, with a small residual probability that the evidence should be regarded as only biological/hypothesized given the absence of identified causal variants.

justification: The clearest primary human evidence is Jen et al. (PMID 16116111), who identified a de novo heterozygous SLC1A3 (EAAT1) missense variant in a single patient with episodic ataxia, seizures, hemiplegia and migraine, with functional loss of glutamate uptake. Other primary SLC1A3 variant reports (PMID 19139306 family with C186S; PMID 27829685 late-onset EA6) describe episodic ataxia explicitly without seizures, so they do not replicate an epilepsy phenotype in independent probands. Additional human support is associative rather than causal: an SLC1A3 tagging SNP (rs4869682) associated with post-traumatic seizure risk after severe TBI (PMID 29999457) and 3'-UTR variants reported in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy RNA-Seq data (PMID 34086756). Strong mechanistic support comes from non-human models — the Slc1a3^P290R/+ mouse with spontaneous EEG-confirmed seizures and impaired tonic GABAergic inhibition (PMID 42563189) and a Drosophila EA6 model (PMID 27445142) — which bolster plausibility but cannot establish human causation. With only one convincing human proband plus associative data, the evidence fits "Existing" rather than "Established."

justification: Multiple independent human families/probands with CHRNA2 variants and seizure phenotypes are reported with primary data: PMID 16826524 (large pedigree with linkage to 8p and I279N, with electrophysiological confirmation), PMID 25770198 (ADNFLE family with I297F segregating in six affected members, loss of function), PMID 30809122 (third independent proband with Y252H, functional characterization), PMID 25847220 (BFIS family with R376W segregating), and a de novo/novel nonsense variant case (PMID 39834405). Several negative screening cohorts (PMIDs 18226955, 26309560, 12195439, 17324557) show that CHRNA2 mutations are rare, which limits frequency but does not undermine causality in the reported families. Hence the relationship is best described as Established, with some residual probability for "Existing" given the rarity and the small number of definitive families.

justification: Human case-control association studies report positive findings for SYN2 intronic variant rs3773364 with idiopathic epilepsy in North Indian (PMID 20034013) and South Indian IGE cohorts (PMID 25088614), and the multicentre EPIGEN candidate-gene study flagged SYN2 among genes with tentative population-specific association (PMID 17913586). However, a tri-ethnic Malaysian case-control study plus meta-analysis found no association (PMID 21465568), making the evidence limited and inconsistent rather than definitive. No study reports causal rare/coding variants in epilepsy probands or families (the SYN2 nonsense/missense mutations reported are in autism, PMID 23956174), so "Established" cannot be supported. Strong supporting biology comes from Syn2 knockout mice that develop seizures and epileptiform activity (PMIDs 35326282, 36870094, 23443540), but these are animal data and only back the hypothesized tier. Overall, human association evidence exists but is not replicated convincingly, so "Existing" is the best fit.

justification: The PDYN promoter 68-bp repeat (low-expression "L" allele) was reported as a susceptibility factor for temporal lobe epilepsy in a human case-control study (PMID 11835385), with partial support in familial/ADLTE cases (PMID 18355961) and two meta-analyses showing significant association restricted to familial-risk TLE (PMIDs 18334734, 26489614). However, several independent replication attempts failed (PMIDs 15888540, 19066720), and the effect is a modest risk allele rather than a causal Mendelian variant; coding PDYN mutations in humans cause SCA23, not epilepsy. Supporting biology (dynorphin/KOR anticonvulsant action, pDyn knockout mice) strengthens plausibility but is largely preclinical (PMID 33712941). This pattern—at least one credible human association study with limited and inconsistent replication—fits "Existing" rather than "Established."

justification: Multiple independent human cohort and family studies report pathogenic SCN1A variants in epilepsy probands with their own primary genetic results: PMID 21248271 (273 laboratory-identified SCN1A mutation carriers plus 546 published cases, with genotype–phenotype correlations), PMID 17347258 (mutation screening of 188 infantile epileptic encephalopathy patients, with mutations in ~79% of SMEI), PMID 34338318 (205 patients with SCN1A pathogenic variants and Dravet syndrome), and PMID 28202706 (182 mutation carriers with phenotypic outcomes). Segregation evidence in a large multigenerational GEFS+ family with a missense variant (PMID 28192756) and non-coding poison-exon variants causing reduced SCN1A protein (PMID 30526861) add independent, mechanistically supported human replication. Population-based incidence data confirm de novo SCN1A mutations as the major cause of Dravet syndrome (PMID 26438699). These are human genetic studies in independent probands/families, not merely background citations or multigene CNVs, so the causal relationship is firmly established.

justification: Several human case-control studies directly report associations between CYP2D6 variants and epilepsy: poor-metabolizer genotypes were over-represented among epileptic patients (PMID 7980640), CYP2D6 2850C>T was associated with generalized tonic-clonic seizures in Indians (PMID 16835697), and CYP2D6*2/*4 variants were associated with epilepsy risk and drug resistance in Egyptian children (PMID 35597526). Additional human studies link CYP2D6 variants to drug-resistant epilepsy or antiseizure-medication outcomes (PMIDs 28343093, 37315635, 39539630, 24338437, 28052106), which are treatment-response/subtype phenotypes rather than causal evidence for epilepsy itself. These studies are small, candidate-gene based, with the plausible mechanism being pharmacokinetic rather than disease-causing, and no families or replicated probands demonstrate causality; a 22q13 deletion case (PMID 20541044) spans many genes and cannot implicate CYP2D6. Therefore the evidence supports "Existing" rather than "Established", with residual probability for a purely biological/pathway (metabolism of antiepileptics) interpretation.

justification: Several papers present their own primary human genetic findings: PMID 24501278 identified a de novo KCND2 p.Val404Met in monozygotic twins with intractable infant-onset seizures plus autism, with functional validation; PMID 35510384 reports an independent de novo p.Val402Leu in a boy with early-onset pharmacoresistant epilepsy evolving to CSWS, again with electrophysiological support; PMID 34245260 describes six unrelated individuals with heterozygous KCND2 missense variants, several with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; and PMID 16934482 reported a Kv4.2 truncation in a temporal lobe epilepsy patient. These are independent probands/families with single-gene point variants (not CNVs), satisfying replication. Supporting mechanistic work (PMID 29581270, and the Kv4.2 V404M knock-in mouse PMID 41554648 showing spike-wave discharges) reinforces causality, while review articles (36225112, 39434833, 29542386) merely restate the association. Residual uncertainty reflects the small number of probands, phenotypic heterogeneity (developmental delay/autism rather than pure epilepsy in some), and uncertain significance of the single TLE truncation report.

justification: Two small human candidate-gene studies report genotypic associations between exonic LGI4 polymorphisms and epilepsy phenotypes: c.1914GC→AT with childhood absence epilepsy (PMID 14505228) and c.1722G/A with benign familial infantile convulsions (PMID 19815358), both based on LGI4's position at 19q13.11 within an epilepsy-linked region; a review restates these as polymorphism-level evidence (PMID 17765802). This meets "Existing" but not "Established": no pathogenic LGI4 variants segregating causally in epilepsy families are reported, sample sizes are tiny, and no replication exists. Indeed, mutation screens in ADPEAF/TLE families and in the 19q13 ADPEAF linkage family found no LGI4 mutations (PMIDs 15079010, 24579982), and a feline epilepsy study found only a benign LGI4 SNP without co-segregation (PMID 29237452). The firmly established human Mendelian phenotype for biallelic LGI4 loss of function is arthrogryposis multiplex congenita with hypomyelination (PMIDs 28318499, 31513940), not epilepsy, so the remaining weight is given to "Hypothesized" based on LGI-family/ADAM22 synaptic and myelination biology.

justification: Direct human variant-level evidence exists in several independent reports: Escayg et al. identified R482X in a JME proband and C104F in a German family with generalized epilepsy/praxis-induced seizures (PMID 10762541); a homozygous p.Leu126Pro variant segregated in two siblings with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, supported by functional work (PMID 32176688); two further unrelated consanguineous Pakistani families carried distinct homozygous missense variants segregating with recessive epilepsy (PMID 42570371); and additional epilepsy cohorts report CACNB4 frameshift/missense variants in patients (PMIDs 35813387, 42037703, 18755274 as a modifier of SMEI). However, substantial doubt remains because a large diagnostic panel study found CACNB4 ultrarare variants at equal frequency in cases and controls and explicitly listed it among genes with contradictory evidence of epilepsy association (PMID 31056551), and much of the remaining literature only cites the association as background (PMIDs 23756480, 16100538, 25893123). justification: Primary human genetic evidence comes from Haug et al. (PMID 12612585), reporting three heterozygous CLCN2 mutations in three unrelated IGE families, Saint-Martin et al. (PMID 19191339) with two novel missense variants in three IGE families, a de novo p.Gly161Ser in a Chinese childhood absence epilepsy patient (PMID 31054517), and biallelic CLCN2 loss-of-function causing leukoencephalopathy with ataxia presenting with seizures (PMID 39779341). However, the causal role in IGE is explicitly contested: several mutation screens found no mutations (PMIDs 16932951, 17580110 only suggestive, 20037607, 19710712), the original variants were reinterpreted as likely polymorphisms with normal function (PMIDs 15252188, 17567819), knockout mice showed no lowered seizure threshold (PMID 17567819), and even the positive report concluded the variants are at most susceptibility factors due to incomplete segregation. Thus the weight of evidence supports a limited/disputed association rather than a replicated, definitive causal link, favoring "Existing," with a sizeable minority probability for "Established" given the recessive leukoencephalopathy cases with epileptic seizures and the de novo CAE variant.
